profile.campus: Metro Atlanta, Georgia (Flexential's Atlanta-market data centers, buildings in Douglasville, Alpharetta, and Norcross)

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Atlanta - Alpharetta Data Center) is located at 12655 Edison Drive, Alpharetta, GA 30022. The operator publishes a footprint of 142,475 square feet and 6 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, SSAE 18. Georgia is projected to waive about $296 million in sales and use taxes for data center equipment this year under two statewide exemption programs, one for large or hyperscale projects (adopted around 2018, modeled on a similar Virginia law) and one for bulk computer equipment purchases; the state has waived at least $163 million annually since 2022, with waivers projected to exceed $327 million by 2026, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution's reporting on state tax-expenditure audits. A 2022 University of Georgia audit found the hyperscale program alone cost the state $5 million in 2018, rising to a projected $57 million by 2030. Georgia is one of 10 states projected to waive nine-figure sums annually through these programs, and in 2024 the state legislature passed a bill to suspend the hyperscale exemption for review, which Governor Brian Kemp vetoed, citing concerns about undermining investment. Metro Atlanta's data center corridor spans several submarkets, including the Douglasville area west of the city (home to Flexential's two largest local buildings), and the Alpharetta/Norcross corridor in the northern suburbs.

Georgia Power's own capacity forecasts illustrate how fast data center demand has grown in the state: the utility projected needing just 400 megawatts of new capacity over seven years in 2022, a figure that jumped to 6,600 megawatts in 2023 and reached 8,500 megawatts by 2025 as data centers proliferated, according to Atlanta Tech News' reporting. In December 2025 Georgia's Public Service Commission approved 9,985 megawatts of new generation, with about 80% of it expected to serve data center demand specifically. The Commission has said data center revenue should reduce rather than increase residential electricity bills, and cited protections including quarterly reporting on new data center activity, longer contract terms with minimum billing so data centers pay for infrastructure even if they relocate, and a Georgia Power financial backstop through 2031 if expected contracts fail to materialize; critics have argued these safeguards remain insufficient and pushed for stronger disclosure and revised tax-incentive terms reflecting current market conditions rather than 2018-era assumptions.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This Flexential cluster spans Georgia (Alpharetta, Douglasville, Norcross), Florida (Fort Lauderdale, Jacksonville, Tampa), North Carolina (Charlotte, Morrisville), and Tennessee (Brentwood, Franklin), the historic Southeastern United States footprint of Peak 10. According to Flexential own company history page, Peak 10 was founded in 2000 and built a strong regional presence across the Southeastern US. In 2017 Peak 10 purchased ViaWest, merging the two regionally dominant data center providers, and the combined company rebranded as Flexential in 2018. Flexential also acquired AppliedTrust and INetU in 2015 to expand its professional services and cloud offerings. Flexential operates 40 plus data centers across 18 national markets under CEO Ryan Mallory. profile.regional_context: Metro Atlanta is one of the largest US data center markets, sustained in part by Georgia's sales-tax exemptions for large data center equipment purchases, a policy that has drawn scrutiny over hundreds of millions of dollars in annual forgone state tax revenue even as it continues to attract large operators to submarkets including Douglasville, Alpharetta, and Norcross.

reading.body:
At 6 MW of published IT capacity across 142,475 square feet of technical space, this campus is a mid-size colocation facility. At 10 kW per rack, a common enterprise colocation density, 6 MW supports roughly 600 racks; at 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, the same load supports roughly 150 racks. The published figure is IT load, not gross building power, so power usage effectiveness overhead is not captured in the 6 MW number. No redundancy tier or cooling architecture is published on the operator's spec page.

The six certifications qualify this campus to host regulated workloads: SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 cover financial and operational controls audited over time, PCI DSS covers payment card data environments, HIPAA covers protected health information, ISO 27001 covers an audited information security management system, and SSAE 18 is the attestation standard underlying the SOC reports. Taken together, the certifications signal a compliance posture suited to enterprise and regulated-industry tenants. Which tenants are actually present is not published.

Among the 33 facilities this site has mapped in Georgia, only 2 have published a megawatt figure, and those two sum to 42 MW. This campus, at 6 MW, ranks second among the two with published figures, representing roughly 14 percent of the state's published IT capacity on this site. That share reflects data scarcity as much as market position: 31 of the 33 mapped Georgia facilities publish no MW figure, so the ranking describes what is visible to this site, not the full Georgia market.
